replying_to: Replying to StatQAT: Statistical Quantizer Optimization for Deep Networks
display_title: Official Review of Submission22605 by Reviewer 2cs9

summary.value:
The paper proposes utilizing analytic quantizers (for weights) and iterative one (for activation) in quantization aware training.
Given the statistics (of weights during QAT), the analytic quantizer for the target data format like FP4 chooses the best quantization parameters (clipping threshold and zero) from pre-computed ones assuming Gaussian distributions.
The experiments show SOTA results.

strengths.value:
The experimental results are quite impressive.
Especially, it looks nice that the proposed method is effective in tensor-wise cases where quantization gets simpler than in channel-wise ones.

weaknesses.value:
Pre-computing quantization parameters based on known distributions and utilizing them (based on the statistics obtained) during QAT is not new.
For instance, in [1], the authors propose an idea called statistics-aware weight binning (SAWB) which quantizes weights based on Gaussian assumption during QAT.

[1] Bridging the Accuracy Gap for 2-bit Quantized Neural Networks (QNN), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.06964

Compared with [1], one key difference will be FP4 since it was not available when [1] was published.
It would be nice to discuss what are 'fundamentally' new problems, in case of FP4, for statistics-aware quantization.
Proposing a statistics-aware method for FP4 based on a floating point-aware analytical analysis (which looks similar to the one in [1] in principle) looks rather weak to me as novelty 
since only number representations are different between Int [1] and Float while the main idea of utilizing the pre-computed results (optimal quantization parameters for a given distribution) looks the same.

questions.value:
It would be nice to explain how the proposed work advances QAT in terms of analytic analyzer 
in comparison with existing QAT works based on analytic quantizers and Gaussian (or pre-determined) distribution assumption.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission22605 by Reviewer 2cs9

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below we provide detailed response to the comment.

***Pre-computing quantization parameters based on known distributions and utilizing them (based on the statistics obtained) during QAT is not new. For instance, in [1], the authors propose an idea called statistics-aware weight binning (SAWB) which quantizes weights based on a Gaussian assumption during QAT. [1] Bridging the Accuracy Gap for 2-bit Quantized Neural Networks (QNN), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.06964. Compared with [1], one key difference will be FP4 since it was not available when [1] was published. It would be nice to discuss what are 'fundamentally' new problems, in case of FP4, for statistics-aware quantization. Proposing a statistics-aware method for FP4 based on a floating point-aware analytical analysis (which looks similar to the one in [1] in principle) looks rather weak to me as novelty since only number representations are different between Int [1] and Float while the main idea of utilizing the pre-computed results (optimal quantization parameters for a given distribution) looks the same.***

We appreciate the reviewer’s comparison to SAWB and agree that statistics-aware quantization is conceptually related. However, our contribution extends far beyond applying existing INT-based ideas to a new number format. FP4 quantization introduces fundamentally different constraints and non-uniform logarithmic spacing, which require a new analytical treatment. Our work provides a detailed and mathematically explicit error decomposition for both uniform and floating-point quantizers, deriving closed-form SNR expressions and lightweight QAT update rules that do not exist in prior INT-focused methods. Importantly, we validate the practical impact of these formulations through an expanded empirical evaluation that includes state-of-the-art LLM baselines and demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple sizes of models. These results highlight that our analytic framework enables high-accuracy QAT in modern large-scale settings.

display_title: Official Review of Submission22605 by Reviewer mHUY

summary.value:
The authors discuss weight and activation quantization in NNs. They analyze the errors of different quantization choices (uniform, FP) and derive a k-means style approach to find appropriately-spaced cluster centers given observed data (weights & activations). They derive iterative and - if data (weights) can be assumed normally distributed - analytical update rules for those cluster centers. 
The authors perform QAT experiments with their proposed methods and compare against baselines.

strengths.value:
This work is well-motivated, the problem of QAT is highly relevant to deploy large models efficiently and the exposition is well-done.
Considering the latency of the quantizer is an important contribution, especially since interative and analytic perform comparably.

weaknesses.value: The only weakness I can identify is the limited empirical evaluation. Looking at e.g. ParetoQ, there is an opportunity to study <4bit quantization - as well as the opportunity to include more models & datasets to improve the robustness of this work.

questions.value:
I believe in EQ 7 the lower limit of the second integral should be $s(N-5/2) + z$
substituting $t_{N-2}=s(N-2-1/2+z)=s(N-4/2-1/2+z) = s(N-5/2+z)$

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and positive feedback. Below we provide detailed responses to each comment.

***The only weakness I can identify is the limited empirical evaluation. Looking at e.g. ParetoQ, there is an opportunity to study <4bit quantization - as well as the opportunity to include more models & datasets to improve the robustness of this work.***

We thank the reviewer for highlighting this opportunity. To strengthen our empirical evaluation, we have added comparisons with LSQ ( LSQ appears under its updated implementation name, ParetoQ, due to the framework we use), a strong and widely used QAT baseline, for 4-bit. Our study focuses on 4-bit quantization because it aligns with the emerging hardware support for FP4 formats (e.g., FP4-E2M1 and FP4-E3M0), which are the primary low-precision targets of current accelerator designs. While <4-bit uniform quantization is an interesting direction, especially in light of results from methods like ParetoQ, it raises additional hardware and representational constraints that go beyond the scope of this work. We therefore leave sub-4-bit quantization as future work.

***I believe in EQ 7 the lower limit of the second integral should be $s(N-5/2) + z$ substituting $t_{N-2}=s(N-2-1/2+z)=s(N-4/2-1/2+z) = s(N-5/2+z)$***

Thanks for catching this up. You are right, and we fixed it.

display_title: Official Review of Submission22605 by Reviewer JukX

summary.value:
The paper proposes StatQAT, a statistical framework for choosing quantization parameters for both uniform and FP schemes.
The core is an analytical decomposition of quantization error into clipping + stepping terms, iterative updates for scale/shift and updates that precompute an optimal clipping constant via SNR maximization, then set per-tensor scales in one shot.
Varius experiments on llms as well as resnet18.

strengths.value:
### Clear error model
for both uniform and floating-point quantizers, including a tractable stepping-error mixture for FP formats (Sec. 3.2, Eqs. 15–16), which is rarely derived cleanly in QAT papers. The SNR-based perspective is useful (Fig. 1, p. 7). 

### Simple, practical update rules
Also shown in appendix how faster the analitical compared to iterative

## Broad Evaluation
Two models with two sizes make the impact broad across models and datasets.

weaknesses.value:
1. The iterative uniform update is essentially a **constrained 1-D k-means** (Lloyd–Max) with fixed spacing , and the FP version mirrors that idea on a scaled FP grid. This feels like a straightforward specialization of classic quantizer optimization to the uniform/FP grids rather than a new algorithmic principle.

2. The “first closed-form analytic solution for FP quantizers in QAT” (Abstract, Intro) seems overstated. optimal **C** is chosen by numerical search on a derived SNR expression (eq 22). Please tone down the claim or clarify precisely what is closed-form.

3. **Positioning vs. prior work** - Prior art already optimizes clipping/scale during QAT (e.g., LSQ/PACT) and analyzes error (Lloyd–Max, optimal clipping). you list  them in the intro, but the manuscript should articulate what is new beyond applying an SNR-driven selection and  demonstrait that a single-step analytic update matches iterative methods under QAT constraints.

4. **Clarity & presentation** - Section 2 is long background, Section 3 sometimes re-derives known pieces (for example, uniform steping error). While i understand that it's improtant for deriving your decomposed error, you can simply reffer to literuture or move to the appendix (similar to some of the solved known integrals you've put there), as it take major part of the paper lenghts.
**Figures** should be PDF and not images, so the quality remain high when zooming, as currently the quality of the figures are poor.

5. Reproducability - I failed to find detalis about the datased you used for fine-tuning the LLMs, with details about it (some QAT uses only the data without labels, or with artificial labels, the size matter a lot since it's much heavier on the saving side of your non iterative suggestion).

6. Where does the gain come from? I would be happy to see more ablations that explain that.. the SNR curves (Fig. 1) suggest robustness/benefit from better clipping. It would help to add per-layer scale histograms, SNR per layer, or an analysis of failure cases vs min-max/LSQ to better understand the effects.

questions.value:
I incorporated my questions in the Weaknesses section.

But regardless, can you provide even a very small scale correlation study why ablation over resnet and cifar translate into LLMs?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below we provide detailed responses to each comment.

***Iterative update resembles constrained Lloyd–Max; seems like a straightforward specialization***

We appreciate the reviewer’s observation and agree that the iterative refinement intuition is related to the classical Lloyd–Max procedure, as we noted in the paper. Our contribution, however, is not the high-level idea of centroid refinement, but the development of a new analytical framework tailored to QAT under hardware-constrained INT4 and FP4 quantizers, which prior work does not address. We derive a detailed and mathematically explicit error decomposition for both uniform and floating-point quantizers, along with closed-form SNR expressions and lightweight single-step update rules that avoid the per-step iterative optimization required by Lloyd–Max or other iterative schemes. These updates are absent in prior INT-based methods and are crucial for practical QAT in large models. We further demonstrate the practical impact of our formulations through expanded empirical evaluations, including state-of-the-art LLM baselines, showing consistent improvements across multiple model sizes. Thus, although the conceptual refinement intuition is shared, the mathematical treatment, datatype-specific constraints, and resulting QAT-compatible updates represent a substantive contribution beyond a straightforward adaptation of Lloyd–Max to uniform or FP grids.

***First closed-form FP QAT solution” seems overstated***

We appreciate the reviewer’s point and have clarified the claim in the revised manuscript. The elements that are closed-form in our method are: (i) the SNR expressions for both uniform and floating-point quantizers given a clipping point, and (ii) the training-time update rules used within QAT. We agree that the optimal clipping point that maximizes SNR under a standard normal assumption does not admit a closed-form solution, and our method therefore uses a lightweight numerical search for this scalar quantity. We have updated the abstract and introduction to reflect this distinction.

***Positioning vs. prior work (LSQ/PACT, Lloyd–Max). Demonstrate novelty***

We thank the reviewer for this observation and have strengthened the positioning in the manuscript accordingly. Prior methods, such as LSQ and PACT, do optimize clipping or scale during QAT, but they rely on gradient-based updates and do not exploit any closed-form structure of the quantization error. Likewise, classical analyses such as Lloyd–Max apply to unconstrained non-uniform quantizers and do not directly extend to the hardware-restricted uniform and FP4 formats targeted in modern accelerators. Our contribution is the derivation of a decomposed quantization error formulation for both uniform and floating-point quantizers, and the resulting single-step closed-form updates for the parameters used during QAT. These updates eliminate the need for iterative optimization of clipping/scale and, as we show empirically, match or outperform iterative methods under the constraints of practical QAT pipelines. We have clarified these distinctions in the revised manuscript related work section.

***Section 2 too long / repeats known results***

We agree that Section 2 was disproportionately long and that some of the background material and re-derived results could be streamlined. In the revised manuscript, we have moved Section 2.4 to the appendix and likewise relocated the derivation of the uniform stepping error to the appendix.  

***Figures should be PDF***

We have regenerated the figures in PDF format.

***Reproducibility: dataset details missing***

We now specify that all LLM QAT experiments use the WikiText-2 train split, following prior work, and use standard unlabeled text for QAT.

***More analysis of where gains come from; more ablations?***

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion to include more diagnostics. In response, we added Appendix I, which reports the per-layer SNR of all linear layers in the Llama-3-1B model under Analytic vs. MinMax quantization. This ablation shows that each layer benefits from better-chosen quantization parameters: Analytic consistently yields higher SNR across layers, indicating more effective clipping/scale selection and reduced quantization error at the layer level. This error reduction then compounds over the forward pass, which explains the improved end-to-end accuracy we observe. While we do not perform a large-scale cross-architecture correlation study, we note that the same qualitative behavior appears in our ResNet + CIFAR ablations: convolution layers that achieve better layer-wise error reduction (higher SNR) also lead to improved final accuracy. This suggests that the mechanism via better clipping and scaling extends beyond a single model family and explains why insights from ResNet/CIFAR ablations carry over to LLMs.

summary.value: The paper demonstrates a statistical framework for optimizing quantization parameters for uniform and floating-point quantization and proposes two quantization procedures, namely, iterative quantizers for arbitrary data distributions (activations) via alternating updates of scale and shift for each time step, and analytic quantizers using a closed form solution for Gaussian-like weight distributions. These methods can be integrated into Quantization-Aware Training (QAT). The method is validated using ResNet, MobileLLM, and Llama 3.2 and the quantizers are compared to minmax and normal quanitzers.

2. Limited comparison - I don't see comparisons with more recent SOTA techniques like SpinQuant for PTQ, LSQ for QAT, etc. 
3. Runs on CIFAR-10 can be noisy, I don't see any characterization of noise.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission22605 by Reviewer XqCB

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below we provide detailed responses to each comment.

***Limited evaluation - the models evaluated are very limited, not clear if the technique will scale to larger models used today beyond ResNet-18 and larger than 3B parameter LLMs. Broader domain coverage could strengthen claims.***

We further included Llama-3 8B in our experiments to show that our results hold across a wide range of model sizes. Due to the significant computational requirements of >8B-parameter models, a thorough evaluation beyond this scale is not feasible for us, but the consistency we observe across small CNNs and mid-sized LLMs suggests the method generalizes. 

***Limited comparison - I don't see comparisons with more recent SOTA techniques like SpinQuant for PTQ, LSQ for QAT, etc.***

Although we appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion, our work focuses specifically on quantization-aware training (QAT), where quantization parameters and model weights are updated during training. Methods such as SpinQuant are designed for post-training quantization (PTQ) and operate under a fundamentally different setting with no original weight updates during training. For completeness within the QAT domain, we have included comparisons with LSQ (implemented within our framework as ParetoQ) and show that our methods achieve superior performance across all evaluated settings. A broader study of how PTQ and QAT approaches interact, particularly hybrid strategies combining SpinQuant-style rotations with analytic QAT updates, is an interesting direction for future work but is beyond the scope of this paper.

***Runs on CIFAR-10 can be noisy, I don't see any characterization of noise.***

We agree that CIFAR-10 runs can exhibit noise, so we repeated each experiment 10 times to characterize variance. The resulting test losses (×10⁻³) are: [6.3 ± 0.21, 5.7 ± 0.15, 5.8 ± 0.11] for minmax, analytic, and iterative quantizers under INT4; and [6.5 ± 0.22, 5.9 ± 0.18, 5.5 ± 0.08] for the corresponding float quantizers. For reference, the full-precision model obtains a loss of 5.0. The small standard deviations across repeated runs indicate that the improvements we report are statistically robust rather than due to random variation.

***The labels used for Fig 2 (left) seem to be incorrect.***

We have regenerated Fig. 2 (left) in higher-resolution PDF format for improved readability and corrected the mislabeled entries. The updated figure in the revised manuscript now uses consistent and accurate labels throughout.

***Can you comment on how this can be combined with existing QAT techniques like LSQ, and include comparisons with some of the techniques mentioned above?***

As noted above, we have included comparisons with LSQ in the revised manuscript to address the reviewer’s request. With regard to combinability, LSQ is itself a full QAT algorithm that introduces gradient-based updates to the quantization parameters. Because our method provides an analytic alternative to these gradient-driven updates, the two approaches effectively serve the same role during QAT and are thus not directly composable within the same training pipeline. Instead, LSQ functions as a baseline against which to compare the effectiveness of our update rules.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission22605 by Area Chair fiEL

summary.value: This paper introduces StatQAT as a statistical framework to optimize the quantization parameters in QAT. It proposes iterative quantizers for activations and analytic quantizers for weight distributions, aiming to reduce error. Three reviewers assigned a score of 4, indicating the paper is marginally below the acceptance threshold. Their primary concerns center on limited novelty, as the core iterative method is seen as a straightforward application of classic Lloyd-Max principles to constrained grids, and claims of a "closed-form" solution are considered overstated. Further weaknesses include a relatively narrow empirical evaluation in terms of model scale and diversity, and insufficient comparison with recent state-of-the-art QAT methods. One reviewer gave a score of 8 but with only fair confidence (3). In their rebuttal, the authors clarified claims regarding "closed-form" solutions, added an experiment with an 8B LLM, included comparisons with LSQ (ParetoQ), provided variance analysis for CIFAR-10 runs, and moved some derivations to the appendix. However, no reviewers give positive response before the rolling back of the OpenReview system.

reviewer_concerns.value: The authors addressed several specific concerns regarding evaluation breadth, figure quality, and mathematical clarifications. However, the central concerns about the fundamental novelty of the approach compared to classical quantization theory and the depth of the empirical validation remain outstanding.

reviewer_scores.value: Given that the authors' rebuttal did not substantively mitigate the core concerns about novelty and evaluation depth raised by Reviewers XqCB, JukX, and 2cs9, it is unlikely their scores would increase after discussion. Reviewer mHUY, who initially scored an 8 with low confidence, might have revised their score downward upon considering the more critical perspectives from other reviewers regarding the contribution's foundation.
